note: Verse 2 says the slips of speech of one praising the faultless are no slips; verse 17 says a fault stays a fault even in those who have reached truth and in a god.
teaches: The fragments hold two standards side by side: the poet excuses faults by the worth of what is praised, while the moral verse refuses to let any height excuse a fault, so the apology rests on devotion, not on a rule about faults.

note: Kural 408 says wealth lodged with the unlearned is more painful than the poverty of the good; 197 says the poet thinks nothing of the riches of the unfeeling and thinks of the poverty of the wise with joy.
teaches: The Kural's comparison is spoken by a poet to a Chola king's face in the Purananuru, which shows that the maxim's ranking of the wise poor over the ignorant rich was first a bard's claim on his own dignity before a patron.

note: Verse 20 bids those who have wealth and pleasure (பொருளடு போகம்) still do austerity; verse 42 says that without austerity the pursuit of wealth and pleasures (பொருளடு போகங்கள்) is fruitless toil.
teaches: The pair make austerity both the duty of the prosperous and the cause of prosperity itself, so wealth and pleasure never stand apart from it.

note: Kural 160 ranks those who fast below those who bear harsh words; Valayapathi 66 calls a vow (நோன்பு) without forbearance (பொறைமை) darkness.
teaches: The Kural only ranks fasting below forbearance, but the fragment makes forbearance the condition without which a vow is worthless, a stronger claim that turns a ranking into a dependence.

gains.a: the fragment's terse item is given the Kural's reason why bearing insult is the harder discipline
gains.b: the couplet's ranking is shown being read by a later epic as a requirement rather than an order of merit

note: Both prize children; the Kural ranks children who come to understanding above all gains, the Valayapathi makes a child the thing without which wealth is like a garland without scent.
teaches: The pairing shows two grounds for the same praise: the Kural values the child for its own understanding, the fragment for completing a householder's estate, so the fragment's child is an ornament of wealth and the Kural's a good in itself.

gains.a: the fragment's list is seen to value the child only in relation to wealth
gains.b: the couplet's condition அறிவறிந்த stands out as what separates its praise from the estate view

note: Both compare a courtesan's love to a river that fails with the rain; the Naladiyar's மாரி அறவே அறுமே and வாரி அறவே அறும் lie close to the Valayapathi's lines 3 and 1.
teaches: The Naladiyar gives only the ending, love cut off when income ends, while the fragment makes வாரி mean both flood and income and adds the rise, so the love is shown swelling with the wealth as precisely as it dries.

gains.a: the fragment is seen reworking a known gnomic comparison, which explains its compression
gains.b: the quatrain's single pun on வாரி proves capable of a full rise-and-fall cycle the quatrain itself leaves out

note: Verse 38 repeats Kural 345 nearly word for word and adds two lines: while the body and ties remain, clinging karma drives the soul through many wombs.
teaches: The couplet's paradox, that even the body is too much for one who would end birth, gets its reason in the fragment: the body is where karma takes hold.

gains.a: the authority of the Kural's own words for its opening
gains.b: an account of why the body is excess, which the couplet asserts without explaining

note: Both start from wealth that will not stay; Naladiyar 2 says share it at once, since it turns like a wheel, while verse 34 praises those who never wanted it.
teaches: The fleetingness of wealth supports two conclusions, the householder's 'give it while you have it' and the renouncer's 'never take it up', and the fragment chooses the more radical one.

gains.a: the householder's alternative, against which its refusal is seen as a choice
gains.b: the renouncer's conclusion from its own premise

note: Kural 334 says what shows itself as a day is a blade sawing through life; Kundalakesi 10 says each day's step takes us to lay our heads at the edge of Death's sword.
teaches: The couplet makes the day itself the blade; the fragment makes the day a step toward a blade held by Death and adds the condemned man's walk, so time becomes not only the cutting but the procession to execution with no reprieve.

gains.a: the fragment's image of the executioner's sword is seen to rest on the Kural's day-as-blade
gains.b: the couplet's still image gains motion and a missing reprieve, which sharpens what 'those who perceive it' would perceive

note: Both say the poor man's well-founded words fail: the Kural's சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும், the Valayapathi's learning that goes புல்லென்று.
teaches: The Kural says only that the poor man's meaning goes slack; the fragment names who lets it, the discerning assembly of the good, and carries the loss from his speech to the learning he teaches.

gains.a: the fragment's complaint is placed as a development of a known Kural rule rather than an isolated grievance
gains.b: the couplet's impersonal 'goes slack' gains named hearers, the good who weigh things, among those who discount the poor

note: Verse 18 states that the wise neither grieve nor exult because what is due will come; verse 19 shows a man unmoved both by a king's pardon and by a plot to kill him, naming all of it the fruit of deeds.
teaches: The maxim of 18 is put to its hardest test in 19, a reprieve and a death plot, and 19 names the cause 18 left unnamed: deeds.

note: Both single out the tongue as what must be guarded above all; the Kural's tongue is speech, the Valayapathi counts it among the five senses and makes it lead to hell.
teaches: Placing the tongue among the senses lets the fragment's warning cover taste as well as speech, so the Kural's rule about words is widened into a rule about appetite, which the fragments' verses on flesh then fill.

gains.a: the fragment's ranking of the tongue is anchored to a well-known rule
gains.b: the couplet's tongue of speech is shown being reread as the tongue of taste too

note: Kural 249 likens virtue done without அருள் to a confused man seeing the truth; Valayapathi 66 lists அருள்இல் அறன் among four goods it calls darkness put inside darkness.
teaches: The Kural makes graceless virtue a single paradox, while the fragment sets it in a series with a vow without forbearance, a lineage without wealth and a kingdom without ministers, so grace appears as one of several enabling conditions without which a good is void.

gains.a: the fragment's one item on grace gains the Kural's fuller case for grace as the root of virtue
gains.b: the couplet's claim is shown to fit a general pattern of goods emptied by a missing condition, which the couplet alone does not show

note: The Naladiyar's wife sets her ever-renewed shyness against women who join many chests for wealth; the Valayapathi says those women serve their payers like பத்தினிப் பெண்டிர்.
teaches: Together they put the difference between wife and courtesan not in the service given, which the fragment says can look the same, but in what the Naladiyar's wife names: a shyness that never wears off and a bond that wealth did not buy.

gains.a: the satirical comparison gains the wife's own account of the inner thing the courtesan only imitates
gains.b: the wife's wonder is sharpened by a text conceding that the courtesan can copy the outward form of her devotion

note: Naladiyar 24 ends with the dying carrying the dead; Kundalakesi 9 says the foetus, child, youth and young adult have each died in us and we die daily.
teaches: The quatrain makes the mourners already dying in the moment of a funeral; the fragment moves death inside each life, as a series of deaths of one's own former selves, so the bearer is also already a corpse many times over.

gains.a: the fragment's interior deaths gain a public scene where the point is seen
gains.b: the quatrain's 'the dying' is given a measure: one dies at every stage of growth

note: The couplet calls the tears of those who cannot bear their suffering a weapon that wears away wealth; here a widow's tears and words take the king's life.
teaches: The couplet's slow wearing-away of a bad king's wealth by the people's tears becomes, in the epic, the instant death of the king at one wronged woman's tears and words.

note: Verse 3 gives the chaste wife public praise and power over rain; verse 4 says any garlanded woman's heart turns to a new man even if she has the love god.
teaches: The surviving fragments hold both the highest claim for a wife's chastity and a denial that any woman's heart stays put, so either the lost story set them in different mouths or it made chastity a rare exception; the conflict depends on reading verse 4 as about all women.

note: Verse 49 puts the பத்தினி among the old courtesan's models; verse 57 explains that model as serving in every way those who give matching wealth.
teaches: Only the gloss in 57 shows why a chaste wife stands in a list of rivers, lutes and beasts: her devotion is taken over as a technique that lasts exactly as long as the payment.

note: Tirumanthiram 1662 makes wearing holy ash the first of the emblems of the flawless Siva-yogi; Kundalakesi 4 puts smearing the body with ash among the practices it calls mere words.
teaches: The same act, ash on the body, is for Tirumular the first sign of the true yogi and for the Kundalakesi a hollow show, so the two traditions disagree on whether an outward mark can belong to tapas at all; the tension depends on reading பொடி பூசல் as ash-smearing.

gains.a: the fragment's target is seen to be a practice a living Tamil tradition held sacred
gains.b: the Saiva emblem is shown under attack from outside, which explains why Tirumular must defend it against hollow wearers

note: Both trace meat back to a price: the Kural says no one would sell flesh if no one killed for eating, the Valayapathi says the eater's craving sets a price at which the trapper kills and sells.
teaches: The Kural makes the buyer answerable for the seller's killing; the fragment adds the trapper's own interest in more deaths, so the guilt runs both ways through the one price.

gains.a: the fragment's hard lines are clarified by the couplet's plainer argument
gains.b: the couplet's one-way blame on the buyer is extended to the seller's motive

note: The Valayapathi argues against flesh-eating in a sermon with no opponent; the Neelakesi announces the view that accepts flesh (ஊன்கொண்ட காட்சி) as the first matter its heroine will debate.
teaches: Among the Jain-tradition epics the same ethic appears in two forms, as a plain moral exhortation in the fragment and as a doctrine to be defended against a named view in the Neelakesi, which shows meat-eating treated as a dividing line between schools and not only as a private fault.

note: Verse 2 praises the one who cut off the three faults without naming them; Kural 360 names three, desire, anger and confusion, whose very names must perish for pain to end.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the epic's unnamed three faults take on a Tamil list already current, and the couplet's goal of ending the three is shown as the very mark by which a Buddhist poet recognises his lord.

gains.a: the fragment's bare 'three faults' gets a known Tamil naming
gains.b: the couplet's triad is seen used as a title of the one who has achieved it, not only a goal for the seeker

note: Both have grey hair as the sign and the staff as age's companion; Naladiyar 11 says the wise renounced in infancy foreseeing grey, verse 36's speaker resolves only after forty, when grey has come.
teaches: The two measure renunciation by when it comes: the quatrain prizes foresight in childhood, while the fragment shows the ordinary case, a man who turns only when desire has already left him.

gains.a: a standard by which its late resolve is the lesser kind
gains.b: a first-person case of the man its wise contrast pass over, showing what makes him turn at last

note: Both poets apologise for faults in their work: the Kundalakesi poet says faults in praise of the faultless one are not faults; the Neelakesi poet says the moon itself has a spot and he will own any fault.
teaches: The two rival works answer the same assembly in opposite ways, the Buddhist denying that his slips count and the Jain conceding them, so the debate between the books begins in how each poet stands toward his own fault.

note: Both deny that women can be kept by outward guarding; the Kural moves the guard inside the woman (நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பு), the Valayapathi says the learned found no guard at all.
teaches: The two share a premise, that confinement fails, and part on the conclusion: the Kural trusts the woman's own steadiness, the fragment trusts nothing, which shows that the Kural's inner guard is a choice and not the only way to read the failure of walls.

gains.a: the fragment's bleak verdict is shown to reject an available answer rather than to lack one
gains.b: the couplet's faith in the woman's own guard is set off by a text that refuses it

note: Parimelazhagar uses Indra to illustrate both verses: 25 for the failure that shows the ascetic's power, and 144 for greatness lost through another's wife.
teaches: This is one story serving two chapters in the commentary, though neither verse tells it.

note: Naladiyar 48 asks whether those who praise sandal paste and garlands have not seen vultures tear the stinking cart of the body; Kundalakesi 12 asks what delight is left in shoulders praised as Mandara when vultures and dogs pluck at them.
teaches: The Naladiyar turns the contemplation of carrion on a body adorned for love, usually the woman's; the fragment turns the same contemplation on a man's heroic shoulders, so the discipline is shown to apply to desire for either sex.

gains.a: the fragment is placed in an established Tamil practice of looking at the body as carrion
gains.b: the quatrain's lesson is shown not to depend on the desired body being a woman's

note: Both liken the woman's fragrance to the kaanthal flowers of Nalli's hill slopes.
teaches: Nalli's hill and its kaanthal were a fixed image for a woman's scent, so a patron's country lent its fame to the beloved's body in more than one poet's hands.

note: Verse 4 says women's hearts melt for another as fish delight in new floodwater; verse 46 says a divided woman's mind can no more be made one than oil spread on water gathered.
teaches: The fragment moves from women's hearts straying to their being past recall once divided, which completes its case for giving them up.

note: Verse 9 says the tongue, among the senses, can send one to the vile hell; verse 19 commands not to eat flesh from craving and promises a good birth.
teaches: Together the two give the tongue's danger a concrete content in these fragments: the craving tongue is the flesh-eating one, and guarding it decides between hell and a spotless rebirth.

note: In Akananuru 151 the woman reports the man's reason that the poor cannot support dependents or laugh among kin, and says his heart has set grace aside; verse 44 gives the same reason, feeding kin's hunger, as one no one could fault.
teaches: The argument for leaving to earn wealth is the same in both, but the akam poem lets the one left behind weigh it against grace, while the fragment's voice treats it as needing no answer.

gains.a: the cost of its argument, borne by the woman left behind
gains.b: a direct statement of the man's case (learning, kin's hunger, the hard road) that the poem gives only as reported speech

note: Verse 37 holds up the farmer who ploughs, sows and waters as the model of provision; verse 42 shows the ploughman who toils without seed as the fool.
teaches: The farmer's image cuts both ways in the fragment: what matters is not the labour, which both farmers do, but whether the seed of austerity was sown.

note: Kural 247 takes as plain fact that this world is not for those without wealth; verse 35 grants that without wealth there is no living but adds that with it base men kill, and that it fails both this world and the next.
teaches: The fragment accepts the Kural's premise and then denies it its consolation: wealth is needed for life and still ruins it, so neither world is secured by it.

gains.a: the Kural's plain premise, which it grants before turning it
gains.b: the dangers of possession that its blunt premise about poverty leaves out

note: Kural 350 commands clinging to the one without clinging in order to let clinging go; verse 39 says removing sin while still in attachment is washing blood with blood.
teaches: If the Kural's holding to the attachment-free one is itself an attachment, the fragment's simile denies that any attachment can cure another, so a release by devotion and a release by pure letting-go part here; the conflict depends on reading the Kural's பற்று as a real attachment.

gains.a: a rival remedy, devotion as the cure of attachment, against which its blood-washing simile becomes a claim
gains.b: a sharp objection that its 'ladder' of attachment must meet

note: Verse 44 makes feeding hungry kin the reason to seek wealth; verse 45 shows the kin scorning and avoiding a man once he is ruined.
teaches: The kin's claim on a man's wealth is not matched by any claim of his on them: their loyalty lasts only as long as the wealth they are owed.

note: Kural 796 finds one benefit in ruin, that it measures one's kin; verse 45 shows that measure taken, the kin speaking as they please and standing out of reach.
teaches: The Kural turns desertion into knowledge for later choices, while the fragment gives the desertion without consolation, so the 'benefit' appears as what it costs.

gains.a: a frame that makes its bitter scene useful knowledge
gains.b: the concrete scene of desertion that its 'measuring rod' implies

note: Both start from crowned kings brought to nothing and rebuke those who see it unchanged: Pattinathar's கண்டு பின்னும், the Valayapathi's கண்டால் மயங்காதே. Pattinathar's way out is reaching the feet of the Lord of the golden hall; the Valayapathi's is standing in the highest path and striving.
teaches: From the same sight the two draw opposed remedies, refuge at a god's feet for the Saiva poet and one's own steady effort for the fragment, which names no god; the tension holds on the reading that the fragment's ஊக்கம் is sufficient by itself.

gains.a: the fragment's call to effort stands out as godless against a Saiva poem built on the same scene
gains.b: Pattinathar's appeal to grace is shown to be one answer to a shared reproach, not the only conclusion the reproach allows

claims.gist: only one who has high birth, a sound body, learning, understanding and dharma deserves the name of human
a courtesan ruins those who trust her most, as a ship drowns those who load it
things whose nature is to perish should not be mourned when they perish
the adorned body will burn in the fire of time
one must not lie or backbite
one must not live by killing creatures and eating them
the body, a product of deeds and a home for worms, cannot be called 'I' or 'mine'
no gift equals a mouthful of food given
without wealth a man is forsaken by wife, kin and even his children
desire can be wiped out by satisfying it
indulgence feeds desire as ghee feeds fire and cannot quench it
what deludes desire is only a covered bag of limbs and fluids that will rot
women keep steady only while their man is watching
grace, not goods, is the wealth to keep, and dharma done with it keeps one from darkness hereafter
the body, foul from every opening and food for dogs, holds nothing sweet to desire
women cannot be managed by skill as kings and snakes can, so the wise renounce them
those who renounce fleeting wealth escape great suffering
a courtesan's love belongs to whoever holds the wealth, not to a person
both lacking and having wealth bring harm, so renouncing it is best
the fruit of theft is mutilation at the king's hands
people gather round wealth and leave when it is gone, whatever a man's birth
truthfulness together with dharma wins a world free of pain
those who keep from mockery and enmity reach heaven
begetting children and keeping household dharma is the highest virtue
a life spent in pleasure with courtesans produces nothing
through the round of births every creature has been one's kin, so eating flesh is eating one's kin
without giving and austerity there is no escape from what follows
the soul passes through many bodies by the force of its deeds, and human birth among them is rare
even a human birth rarely brings wealth enough to enjoy
love grown deep-rooted drives a man to base public folly
a dharma that involves killing is to be refused
one must not despise the poor
one must not approach another man's woman
the faultless vision of the Nirgrantha sages removes sorrow
one must show grace to every living being
these virtues are to be kept as one's wealth
one who lacks true knowledge cannot guide another to release, however much he promises to remove past faults
killing living beings binds one to wander among the four states of birth
desire overrides judgment and the counsel of the wise
one struck by desire loses shame, ignores elders and ruins his fame
a courtesan leaves a man when his wealth is gone and moves to a richer one
Death spares no one, though beings have served him through endless births

note: Pattinathar asks what use weeping is, since good and evil will not come otherwise than as the lotus-born god wrote; Kundalakesi 19 has a man stay unmoved by pardon and death because all that befalls is the fruit of deeds.
teaches: Both counsel the same steadiness, but the Siddhar grounds it in what a god wrote and the fragment in one's own deeds, so the same calm rests on incompatible accounts of who decides what comes.

gains.a: the fragment's karma is set against a theistic account of the same events
gains.b: the Siddhar's appeal to Brahma's writing is shown to be one choice among Tamil grounds for equanimity

note: Naladiyar 48 asks whether those who praise sandal and garlands have not seen vultures tear the corpse; Valayapathi 70 says the heart, though it sees the adorned hair burn, is still bewildered.
teaches: The Naladiyar treats delight in adornment as ignorance that the sight of the corpse would cure, while the fragment's heart has already seen the burning and is bewildered still, so the pair separates not knowing the body's end from knowing it to no effect.

gains.a: the fragment's lament is sharpened by a verse that still trusts sight to cure desire
gains.b: the quatrain's appeal to what one has seen is shown to have a limit, a heart that sees and is unmoved

note: Both use the fresh flood (புதுப்புனல், வெள்ளம் புதியது) for women's love; in the Naladiyar it is the courtesan's love that dries when the money stops, in the Valayapathi it is the new water the fish leave the old pond for.
teaches: The image changes its target: the Naladiyar confines the fickle flood to women whose love is bought, while the fragment turns it on any woman, even one with a perfect lover, so the charge moves from the market to the marriage.

gains.a: the fragment's fish-and-flood image is seen as a reworking of an existing figure of fickle love
gains.b: the quatrain's limitation of the charge to paid women stands out against a text that drops it

note: The fragment states that a thief's fruit is to be seized and cut; the Pandya tells Kannaki that killing a thief is no cruel sceptre, then finds he heeded a goldsmith and was himself the thief.
teaches: The rule that theft earns the king's punishment holds only when the thief is truly known; the epic shows the same rule, unexamined, turning the punisher into the criminal.

note: Both speak of a handful or mouthful of food set aside as a gift; Tirumular says anyone can give it, the Valayapathi says no gift equals it.
teaches: The same small gift is easy in the Tirumanthiram and supreme in the fragment, and held together they say that the gift no one can excuse himself from is also the one no greater gift surpasses.

gains.a: the fragment's obscure gesture of a finger set on a mouthful is matched to a known practice of setting food aside before eating
gains.b: the Saiva verse's minimum gift gains a claim to the highest rank among gifts

note: The fragment takes over Kuruntokai 17's palm-horse, erukku garland, jeering street and heartwood-hard love, and adds baseness, possession and disease.
teaches: The same four acts that the Sangam lover names as love's compulsion, in his own voice, become in a renunciant work the symptoms of a sickness to be avoided: the change of speaker is what changes the verdict.

gains.a: the source of its catalogue, which shows that the 'disease' was once a lover's threat to win his woman
gains.b: an outsider's moral reading of its acts, which the lover's own speech never gives

note: The courtesan leaves the man whose wealth has perished for a richer one, like a beast moving to a fresh field; in 65 all followers leave a man whose wealth is spent, like birds from a fallen fruit tree.
teaches: Read beside 65, the courtesan's switching is not her special vice but one case of the rule the fragments state for kin and followers alike, so the satire of the courtesan rests on a general claim that people follow wealth.

note: Kural 377 says even hoarders of millions enjoy only as the apportioner apportioned; verse 42 says that without the seed of austerity the toil for wealth and pleasure bears nothing.
teaches: Both deny that effort alone secures enjoyment, but the Kural names an apportioning agent while the fragment puts the cause in one's own past austerity, a karma without a giver.

gains.a: the point that its seed is a form of apportioning, set against a rival account of who apportions
gains.b: a cause without a personal agent, which makes its வகுத்தான் visible as a choice

note: 16 asks whether the queen's bed will escape loneliness while the king lingers in camp; 19 says his love of war leaves no grace even for his modest wife, who has him only in dreams on the rare night he sleeps.
teaches: Taken together, the two poems show the decade returning to the queen's cost of war as a counter-voice inside praise, and 19 sharpens the question of 16 into a charge, set beside the ruin of the enemy's farmers.

note: Kural 957 says a fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon; Kundalakesi 17 says a fault stays a fault even in those who have reached truth, as the stain on the god's throat is still a stain.
teaches: The couplet says height makes a fault more visible; the fragment adds that height does not change its nature, and carries the rule up from the well-born to the gods.

gains.a: the fragment's claim is grounded in the Kural's moon-spot observation
gains.b: the couplet's rule is extended beyond human lineage to the divine

note: The Naladiyar's bees do not go to the hill when the kanthal is not in flower; the Valayapathi's birds circle a fruiting tree and leave it when it falls.
teaches: The Naladiyar shows only the loss, that the poor have no kin, while the fragment adds the converse, a servant with food surrounded and a noble without it deserted, so the pair shows wealth outranking birth in both directions.

gains.a: the fragment's bird image is matched by the nature image an ethical anthology used for the same claim
gains.b: the quatrain's one-way rule gains its converse, that the low-born with wealth win the following the poor lose

note: Kural 60 calls good children the ornament of a home's excellence; Valayapathi 61 calls begetting children and keeping household dharma the chief virtue, and a life with deceitful women barren.
teaches: The fragment turns the Kural's praise of children into an argument against the courtesan: her union is measured by the household's fruit, children, and found to yield nothing.

gains.a: the fragment's verdict on the courtesan's life is grounded in the Kural's ranking of the household's goods
gains.b: the couplet's praise of children gains a counter-case showing what a life without the household's ornament is judged to lack

note: Both use the blind guiding the blind for a false teacher of release: the Valayapathi's அந்தகன் அந்தகற்கு ஆறு சொலல், Tirumular's குருடர்க்குக் கோல்காட்டிச் செல்லும் குருடர்.
teaches: Tirumular's blind guide fails for want of a true guru's sight, while the fragment names the missing thing as full knowledge in one who promises to clear past faults, so one proverb serves both a guru-centred and a knowledge-centred account of release.

gains.a: the fragment's unnamed false teacher is set beside a worked-out Saiva doctrine of the false guru, which shows how common the charge was
gains.b: Tirumular's image gains a witness outside Saivism in which the blind guide lacks knowledge that clears past deeds, not a guru's grace

note: Kural 297 says unbroken truthfulness makes all other virtues unnecessary; verse 28 pairs giving up falsehood with practising dharma and promises a painless world for both.
teaches: Truth can be held as the whole of virtue or as one ornament worn with the rest; the fragment takes the second view and pays for it with a promise of the next world that the Kural does not make.

gains.a: the Kural's sharper claim, against which its pairing of truth and dharma shows as a choice
gains.b: a reward named for the truthful, where the couplet only ranks virtues

note: Both rest on what the knowing say (என்ப; கூறினர் அறிந்தார்): Kural 330 reasons from a wretched life back to killing; verse 30 names the four states of birth as killing's issue.
teaches: The fragment supplies the cosmology, the Jain four states of birth, that the couplet's backward inference from suffering to killing needs but never states.

gains.a: a statement of the harsh inference its rule implies: that the wretched now are killers before
gains.b: an explicit rebirth scheme in place of its bare 'they say'

note: Kural 379 asks why those who welcome good when it comes should grieve when it does not; Kundalakesi 18 says those who know that what is due will come neither grieve nor exult.
teaches: The couplet only rebukes grief and leaves joy at good fortune untouched; the fragment strikes out elation too, so its equanimity is stricter than the Kural's.

gains.a: the fragment is seen as answering a question the Kural poses
gains.b: the couplet's one-sided rebuke is shown to stop short of the full equanimity its premise allows

note: Both set the wealth of grace (அருள்) above wealth of goods; the Kural argues from distribution (goods are found even among the base), the Valayapathi commands that grace be made the wealth and ties it to escape from darkness hereafter.
teaches: The Kural gives the reason grace outranks goods, and the fragment gives the practice and its fruit, turning a valuation into a command with an afterlife reward the couplet does not mention.

gains.a: the fragment's command gets the argument that justifies its ranking
gains.b: the couplet's ranking is shown carried into a promise about the next world

note: Kural 346 says the one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' enters a world above the gods'; Kundalakesi 14 asks whether a body of deeds, fed on by worms, can be called 'I' and 'mine'.
teaches: The couplet gives the reward for cutting 'I' and 'mine' but not the argument; the fragment gives the argument from the body's foulness and tenants but promises no higher world, so together they separate the case against 'mine' from the hope it is made for.

gains.a: the fragment's question is seen to aim at a goal the Kural names
gains.b: the couplet's bare command gains a reason a hearer can test on his own body

note: The Naladiyar makes the flesh-eater's belly a burning ground for beasts and birds; the Valayapathi, through rebirth, makes the beasts eaten the eater's own kin.
teaches: Put together, the eater's belly becomes a burning ground for his own relatives: the fragment supplies the kinship the quatrain's image lacks, and the quatrain supplies the funeral the fragment's argument implies.

gains.a: the fragment's kinship argument gains a vivid image of where the kin end up
gains.b: the quatrain's burning-ground image gains a reason why the dead in it are mourned as one's own

note: Acharakkovai 10 makes bathing the removal of impurity on ten occasions; Sivavakkiyar addresses those who bathe daily and whose dirt never goes, asking where the dirt really lies.
teaches: The Siddhar denies the premise the bathing list rests on, that the impurity is where water can reach, whereas the Kural only ranks it below inner purity.

note: Naladiyar 183 bids one sow seed for the next life without confusion; verse 37 makes it a farmer's whole round, ploughing, sowing and watering, always and always.
teaches: Seed for the next life is not one act of sowing but a continuing labour, and the fragment spells out the farming year the quatrain compresses into a word.

gains.a: the explicit term மறுமைக்கு வித்து that names what its farmer is sowing
gains.b: the full labour of the field, which turns its single command into a discipline

note: Verse 5 says the knowing found no guard for women though food, wealth and learning can be guarded; verse 26 says no art manages them as kings and snakes are managed, so the wise let them go.
teaches: Read together, the two verses carry the claim from 'women cannot be kept' to its renunciant conclusion, 'so give them up'.

note: Both say rain falls at the chaste wife's word; the Kural makes it her one power, the Valayapathi sets it in a list of honours with the praise of country and town and credits it to what the learned of Koodal say.
teaches: Read beside the fragment, the Kural's single astonishing claim becomes an item of public reputation, cited on authority, so the rain is treated as the community's recognition of the wife rather than her private power.

gains.a: the fragment's rain-claim is anchored to the couplet that first stated it
gains.b: the couplet's claim is seen being received as a cited saying and folded into public honour

note: Kural 280 says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Kundalakesi 4 dismisses a longer list, nakedness, ash, cold, fire, alms and matted hair, as words, and calls tapas a subdued life.
teaches: The couplet sets aside only the hair, and tests the renouncer by the world's blame; the fragment sets aside the whole repertoire of bodily austerity and puts the test in inner restraint, so the two differ on where the renouncer's proof lies.

gains.a: the fragment's dismissal is seen to extend a point the Kural already made about outward marks
gains.b: the couplet's narrow example is shown to open onto a general attack on bodily penance

note: Both tell of a man whom desire strips of shame and standing; the Kural's lover says it in his own voice as a loss of shame and manliness, the Valayapathi condemns it from outside as blame and stained fame.
teaches: The same loss is a lover's plea in the Kural and a moralist's charge in the fragment, so the pair shows the madal lover judged two ways: as one whose suffering should move his beloved, and as one whose reputation is ruined.

gains.a: the fragment's censure is set against the lover's own account it ignores
gains.b: the couplet's inventory of loss is shown as it looks to the society the lover defies

note: Both make women's faultless time short; the Naladiyar says even under a guard of swords, the Valayapathi says only while the man who cherishes them is watching.
teaches: On whether watching helps, the two disagree: for the fragment, the provider's gaze buys a brief steadiness, while for the quatrain even armed guard does not, so the fragment's distrust is milder in what it allows surveillance to achieve.

gains.a: the fragment's raindrop image is placed in a tradition of harsh sayings and measured against it
gains.b: the quatrain's claim that guarding fails is shown to be stronger than a parallel text's

note: Kural 1047: one whose poverty has no virtue is looked on as a stranger even by his mother; Valayapathi 63: without wealth, a man's women disregard him, his kin shrink, and his own children will not cling.
teaches: The Kural limits its harsh rule to poverty without அறம் and names only the mother, while the fragment drops the limit and extends the desertion to wife, kin and children, which shows how far the claim reaches once its moral condition is removed.

gains.a: the fragment's sweeping claim is seen to lack the qualifying condition the Kural attaches
gains.b: the Kural's qualifier அறஞ்சாரா is shown to do real work once a version without it stands beside it

note: Both put not killing above ritual merit; the Kural says abstaining from one killing is better than a thousand oblations, the Valayapathi refuses any dharma that comes with killing.
teaches: The Kural weighs non-killing against sacrifice and finds it heavier, while the fragment denies that a killing rite is dharma at all, so the pair shows the step from ranking merits to disqualifying a kind of virtue.

gains.a: the fragment's flat refusal is seen as a sharpening of an older comparison
gains.b: the couplet's comparison is shown to stop short of the verdict a later text draws

note: 393: the bard's family sings lineages by inherited order (குடிமுறை பாடி) and asks the king for food and cloth; Kural 1062 curses the maker of the world if anyone must live by begging.
teaches: What the Kural treats as an outrage against the world's order, a life that depends on asking, the bard presents as a hereditary office with its own proper order of song, so the two disagree on whether living by the gift is a shame or a calling.

note: Verse 33 says poverty is disgrace and wealth fear, so those who never approach wealth are best; verse 44 asks what shame there is in crossing the wasteland for wealth that feeds one's kin.
teaches: Set side by side by the anthology's editor, the two answer the same question opposite ways: whether the duty to feed kin makes the pursuit of wealth honourable or only another snare.

note: Verse 7 says the wise do not mourn things whose nature is to perish and calls weeping from love a self-injury; verse 9 asks why we do not weep for ourselves, who die day by day.
teaches: The call to weep in 9 cannot be the grief that 7 forbids: it is a rhetorical shock meant to make the living see their own dying, so the fragments separate mourning others from waking to one's own mortality.

note: Purananuru 192 says good and ill do not come from others, we neither delight in life nor call it bitter, since life moves by its order like a raft on a river; Kundalakesi 18 says what is due comes, so the wise neither grieve nor exult.
teaches: The Sangam poet draws from the same certainty a rule about others, neither marvelling at the great nor despising the small; the fragment draws only the inner rule, so the pair shows one premise yielding a social ethic in one book and a private discipline in the other.

gains.a: the fragment's maxim gains an older Tamil statement of the same order of things
gains.b: the Sangam poem's equanimity is shown carried into a later religious setting where it becomes a teaching on grief and joy

note: Pattinathar's verse has fire, worm, earth, kite, jackal and dog each say of the body 'it is mine'; Kundalakesi 14 says worms feed and live in the body while one still calls it 'mine'.
teaches: The fragment finds the rival owners already at work in the living body, while Pattinathar lines them up at the corpse; held together, the claim 'mine' is false both before death and after it.

gains.a: the fragment's denial is extended past death to every scavenger
gains.b: the Siddhar's after-death scene is shown to have begun in the living body, which sharpens his question of what gain the rearing brought

note: Kural 1148 says thinking gossip can put out love is like thinking ghee can put out fire; Kundalakesi 5 asks whether a fire-pit can be put out with ghee, of those who would end desire by enjoying it.
teaches: The same proverb of ghee on fire serves the lover, for whom nothing will quench love and that is its strength, and the ascetic, for whom indulgence only feeds desire and that is its danger.

gains.a: the fragment's argument is seen to borrow an image already fixed in love poetry and turn it
gains.b: the couplet's image is shown to carry a warning against desire that the love-speaker does not draw

note: Both call the human body rare (அரிய, அரும்பெறல் யாக்கை); the Valayapathi derives the rarity from karma's long series of bodies, the Naladiyar draws the duty of pressing virtue from it.
teaches: The Naladiyar's command to use the rare body gains its urgency from the fragment's account of how many karma-driven bodies come before a human one, and the fragment's second rarity, wealth to enjoy, is what the quatrain says to turn into virtue instead.

gains.a: the fragment's statement of rarity gets the practical conclusion it leaves unsaid
gains.b: the quatrain's bare 'rare body' is given its cause in the cycle of deeds

note: The Valayapathi says hard penance fit for grace leads to the dark-free state of no return; Tirumular says even burning one's bones and frying one's flesh does not reach the Lord without love that melts.
teaches: The two disagree on whether one's own austerity reaches the goal: the fragment's release needs no god and comes by penance, while the Tirumanthiram makes the most extreme penance worthless without love for the Lord; the conflict holds if the fragment's தவம் is read as sufficient by itself.

gains.a: the fragment's godless route to release is set against the strongest Saiva denial of it
gains.b: Tirumular's dismissal of austerity is seen answering a real rival claim, not an abstract one

note: 741 allows that a ruler may fear and protect himself behind walls. 775 counts even a blink before a spear as flight.
teaches: The chapter on the state and the chapter on the warrior hold different standards for fear, and both are the Kural's.

claims.gist: one who stands in the highest path and strives will reach attainment
faults of wording in praise of the one who cut off the three faults are not to be counted as faults
only the perfected ascetic fully ends delusion and restrains mind, speech and body
of the five senses the tongue most needs guarding, since it can raise a man or send him to hell
not desiring wealth at all is the true strength
the lord to take refuge in is the one who, from first to last, thought only good, spoke only virtue and toiled for others with no thought for himself
wealth, had or lacked, is barren for this world and the next
desire is removed by union
the fire of desire is quenched only by the water of revulsion
a certain vice brings ignorance, poverty, affliction and habitual lying
a woman's divided mind cannot be made single again
a man who keeps to his wife is praised on earth and welcomed by the gods
dharma without grace, a vow without forbearance, lineage without wealth and kingship without ministers are void
a courtesan's love is made to wane as surely as it was made to grow
each day is a step without return toward death, so living is a march to execution
countless men who believed they had won a woman's heart were deceived
no sin is greater than killing a life wrongly
the eater's craving and the seller's price together drive the killing of animals
all purity depends on turning toward the pure one who has no thought of evil deeds
as long as body and attachment remain, karma clings and drives the soul through many births

echoes.words: மற்றும் தொடர்ப்பா(டு) எவன்கொல் பிறப்(பு)அறுக்கல் உற்றார்க்(கு) உடம்பு மிகை

claims.gist: sin born of attachment cannot be removed while one keeps attachment
going to another man's woman brings on heavy deeds; avoid it whatever comes
one who protects life, refuses flesh and gives up anger is reborn in a good state
desire for a body is undone by seeing it as carrion for vultures and dogs
wealth without a child is incomplete
kin desert and scorn one who is ruined
poverty makes even true learning go unvalued
a courtesan's devoted service imitates the chaste wife's but follows the payment
since youth does not last, renunciation should follow when age comes
a courtesan's love rises and falls exactly with the lover's wealth
wealth is lost in many ways, and those who let it go without clinging escape its grief
the chaste wife earns public praise, and rain falls at her bidding
seeking wealth across hard country is honourable because it feeds one's kin
a fault remains a fault even in those who have reached truth and in gods; greatness does not make it good
one dies daily, each stage of life dying into the next
a woman's heart turns to someone new however worthy her man
what is due will come, so the wise neither grieve at loss nor exult at gain
without the seed of austerity, toil for wealth and pleasure yields only suffering
all that befalls one is the fruit of one's deeds
going without clothes is a practice of tapas
bodily mortifications such as ash, cold water, fire, alms and matted hair make up tapas
true tapas is a restrained, subdued way of living, not bodily display
women cannot be guarded by any means a man has
merit for the next birth must be cultivated continually, as a farmer tends his field
hard penance with grace leads to a state from which there is no return to birth
